# Exact reductions for a triangle signed-area problem

This note does not prove the final signed-area inequality. It reduces
its two geometric cases without assuming an extremizer or a polygonal
classification.

Normalize the triangle to

    K={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=3}, g=(1,1).

The three negative triangles are

    D_01=conv{(1,0),(2,0),g},
    D_02=conv{(0,1),(0,2),g},
    D_12=conv{g,(1,2),(2,1)}.

Write D for their union and J(Q)=|Q|-3|Q intersect D|.
Their interiors are disjoint; each has area 1/2. The three remaining
positive cells, disregarding null boundaries, are parallelograms E_i
of area one. The desired inequality is J(Q)<=1 for every compact
convex Q subset K.

## A. A chord reduction when g belongs to Q

Initially suppose g is interior to Q. Each negative triangle is the
intersection of K with a cone W_j based at g. Let p_j,q_j be the outer
intersections of Q with its two bounding rays. Let L_j be the closed
halfplane containing g bounded by the line p_j q_j.

Then Q outside W_j is contained in L_j. To check this, use coordinates
along p_j-g and q_j-g, so that the two outer ray intersections have
coordinates (1,0),(0,1), and L_j is a+b<=1. A point of Q outside the
cone that violates this inequality has, say, a<0 and b>1-a. Its segment
to (1,0) meets the other positive ray at b/(1-a)>1, contrary to the
choice of that ray endpoint. The case b<0 is symmetric. Both coordinates
cannot be negative for a+b>1.

It follows that cutting Q by L_j removes points only from D_j, hence
cannot decrease J. Moreover L_j intersect W_j is exactly the triangle
conv{g,p_j,q_j}, which is already contained in Q.

Set

    P=K intersect L_01 intersect L_02 intersect L_12.

All the original six ray endpoints remain in all three halfplanes:
for a different cone they lie outside its interior, where the preceding
argument applies. Thus Q'=Q intersect all L_j has, in each D_j, precisely
the same triangular portion as P. The inclusion Q' subset P therefore
adds positive area only. Consequently

    J(Q)<=J(Q')<=J(P).

This proves an exact reduction to three halfplane cuts. It does not
assert that arbitrary choices of six ray radii are feasible, nor that
the resulting finite parameter optimization has been solved.

If g is on the boundary of Q, set Q_epsilon=(1-epsilon)Q+epsilon K.
These convex sets lie in K, contain g in their interior, and converge to
Q in Hausdorff distance. Their indicators converge outside the boundary
of Q when Q has interior, and their areas tend to zero otherwise. The
same assertions for intersections with the fixed triangles D_j follow
by the nullity of boundaries of full-dimensional convex sets and bounded
dominated convergence. Hence J(Q_epsilon) tends to J(Q). Any universal
upper bound established for the three-halfplane replacements would thus
extend to this boundary case without requiring the replacement parameters
themselves to converge.

## B. A trapezoid reduction when g does not belong to Q

A strict separating affine functional through g is positive on Q.
Write this functional, after subtracting its value at g, as
sum_i a_i(lambda_i-1/3), where lambda_i are the three barycentric
coordinates. In the exclusive cell E_i one has
lambda_i-1/3>0 and lambda_j-1/3<0 for j different from i.
Choose i with a_i minimal. On E_i the separating functional equals

    sum_{j different from i}(a_j-a_i)(lambda_j-1/3)<=0.

Thus Q misses the interior of at least one exclusive cell. Intersecting
Q with the trapezoid spanned by the other two exclusive cells removes
only negative area, so cannot decrease J. By an affine symmetry of K
this trapezoid can be taken as

    H={(x,y):0<=y<=1, 0<=x<=3-y}.

Inside H the negative region is the triangle

    0<=y<=1, 1<=x<=2-y.

For a compact convex Q subset H, its horizontal sections are intervals
of lengths w(y) on an interval I subset [0,1]. The function w is
nonnegative and concave on I and obeys w(y)<=3-y.

Replace each section by [0,w(y)]. This gives the convex compact set
Q_left={(x,y):y in I,0<=x<=w(y)} and preserves area. For an interval of
length w inside [0,3-y], its overlap with the middle interval [1,2-y]
is at least

    min(1-y,(w-1)_+).

Indeed, if it does not meet both outer intervals, its positive portion
has length at most one; if it does meet both, it contains the whole
middle interval. The displayed lower bound is attained by [0,w].
Thus J(Q_left)>=J(Q), and

    J(Q_left)=integral_I [w(y)-3 min(1-y,(w(y)-1)_+)] dy.

It would therefore suffice in this case to prove that the last integral
is at most one for every such concave width function. That one-dimensional
inequality is not proved in this note.

For reference, its integrand also equals

    w-3(w-1)_+ +3(w+y-2)_+.

Both equality examples w=1 and w=3-y on [0,1] give integral one.
These examples do not constitute a classification of its maximizers.
